new_statements.quote: [p. 1] The number of inventory of phonemes is twentyseven: twentyfive segmental and two supra-segmental phonemes. The segmental phonemes are (1) six vowel phonemes and (2) nineteen consonant phonemes. The supra-segmental phonemes are the two tones (1.1.2). [p. 19, §1.4.2 Tones] The two tones set up in the previous sections (1.1.2), (1.2.2) and (1.3.2) can occur both in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words. But when two vowels occur in sequence they (tones) are always marked differently - the first member is invariably falling, the second member is rising and vice-versa, except /u/ which has the same tone (see 1.4.1.2).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Maram is described as a two-tone language (falling vs. rising, contrastive on every syllable, e.g. /ammi/ 'fire' vs. 'goat', /aba/ 'debt, back' vs. 'dung, hand'); tone is the only suprasegmental phoneme recognised. The grammar never mentions word stress or accent, in the phoneme inventory, the symbols list, the syllable chapter or elsewhere, so no stress rule can be extracted; the language enters the catalog as tonal with no stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tonal: in a sequence of two vowels the tones must differ (falling+rising or rising+falling), except that /u/ keeps the same tone (§1.4.1.2, 1.4.2). Aspiration contrast noted as rare and needing further investigation (p. 1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: tones 'can occur both in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words'; data are the spoken language of Maram Khullen village, taken by the author as the standard of all Maram dialects (Introduction). Falling and rising tones written as grave/acute over the vowel in citation forms and in the Appendix vocabulary.
new_statements.identity_note: Singh 1984 analyses the speech of Maram Khullen village, which the author takes as the standard for all Maram dialects; this corresponds to Glottolog dialect Maram Khullen Circle [mara1380] under Maram Naga [mara1379]. Author name appears as 'Pebam, Ibopishak Singh' on Shodhganga and 'Singh, Pebam Ibopishak' in Glottolog (same person). The Shodhganga thesis 'Some aspects of Maram dialect of West Khasi hills' (10603/169676) concerns a Khasi variety, not this language.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the saved text layers under (no refetch; handle https://shodhganga.inflibnet.ac.in/handle/10603/703856 returned HTTP 200 on 2026-09-18). Printed folios in the extracted text output bracket each passage. (1) line 47, between folio 38 (line 37) and folio 39 (line 75) = p. 39, §2.1: 'The language under study has a total of thirty-four phonemes, out of which twenty-nine are segmental and five are suprasegmental, viz., tone.' verbatim. (2) line 133, between folio 86 and folio 87 = p. 87: 'carries the primary phonological load for stress and contrastive tone (Mortensen, 2023)' verbatim, in the general 'Sesquisyllables' paragraph (minor syllable 'never carries contrastive tone or stress').…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Singh 1984: tone language, no stress statement). Adds that the minor syllable of sesquisyllables is unstressed and the final major syllable is the locus of prominence and lexical tone, and that intensity/duration are not contrastive. It differs from Singh 1984 on the tone inventory (five tones vs Singh's two, 34 phonemes vs 27), which is a tone-count disagreement, not a stress disagreement. Same variety as Singh (Maram Khullen).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Maram is a tone language with five lexical tones (H, M, L, mid-rising, low-rising); the thesis states no word-stress rule and has no stress/accent section. Its only stress statements concern sesquisyllables: the initial minor syllable (Cə- or a syllabic nasal) is 'reduced, unstressed' and never carries tone or stress, while the following major (final) syllable is the tone-bearing, prominent syllable; the general characterisation on p. 87 ('the major syllable.. carries the primary phonological load for stress and contrastive tone') is a typological statement citing Mortensen 2023, then applied to Maram on p. 89. In disyllables the first syllable is tone-neutral and the second/final syllable carries the tonal contrast (ch. 4, pp. 148-149; ch. 7 p. 256); intensity and duration are not tonal cues (p. 150). So the only prominence pattern stated is right-edge (final major syllable) in sesquisyllabic and compound words, expressed through tone, not through a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. On tone: compounds neutralise medial and contour tones while edge (final) tones stay intact (ch. 5, ch. 7 pp. 256-257); affixes are toneless and take polar tone from the root.
new_statements.identity_note: Joanna 2026 describes the Maram Khullen dialect, fieldwork in Lairouching village, Senapati district, Manipur, by a native-speaker author (ISO nma); the thesis places Maram in Kuki-Chin (p. 259). Singh 1984, the existing catalog source, also takes Maram Khullen village speech as standard. Joanna cites Mishra 2007 on the Tumuyon Khullen dialect (not opened here, not in the works list).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress: neither Singh 1984 (existing statement) nor Joanna 2026 states a word-stress rule, and both treat Maram as a tone language. They disagree on the tone inventory: Singh 1984 sets up two tones (falling, rising; 27 phonemes), Joanna 2026 five (high, mid, low, mid-rising, low-rising; 34 phonemes, pp. 39, 163-164). Joanna 2026 adds a weak prominence statement (minor syllable of sesquisyllables unstressed; final major syllable bears tone and prominence) that Singh lacks; this is compatible, not contradictory.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere: ch. 1 Phonology sets up 27 phonemes = 25 segmental + 2 suprasegmental, the suprasegmentals being two tones (falling, rising; §§1.1.2, 1.2.2, 1.3.2, 1.4.2), then syllable structure (§1.5); the Symbols page lists no stress mark; a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned text of all chapters for stress/accent/prominence/loud gives no hit. Tones occur in mono- and polysyllabic words; in vowel sequences the two tones must differ (p. 19).
